pos: n. phr. (solid food, as opposed to milk; the deeper doctrine fit for the mature)
etymology: English strong + meat, the older English word for food of any kind, not flesh only; rendering Greek sterea trophē, solid nourishment, from stereos, firm or hard.
biblical_def: The writer to the Hebrews rebukes his readers for a stalled appetite: “For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.” Meat in the Authorized Version is food of any sort, and strong meat is solid food as against liquid — the Greek is sterea trophē, firm nourishment. The figure is developmental and the rebuke is about time. Milk is right for a baby and wrong for a man who has been at the table for years. The charge is not that these readers are young but that they ought by now to be teachers and still require teaching. Two marks of the two diets are given. Of milk: “every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.” Of strong meat: it “belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.” The faculty of discernment is trained by reason of use — it is a worked capacity, grown by exercise, not a temperament some believers are born with. Paul uses the same figure with the Corinthians, having fed them with milk because they were not able to bear meat. In both apostles the point is identical: there is a deeper course of doctrine, it is meant for ordinary Christians, and the failure to reach it is a fault to be repented of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Meat, food in general; that which is eaten for nourishment. Strong meat, Hebrews 5:12, solid food as distinguished from milk; figuratively, the deeper doctrines of the faith.
webster_full: Meat, food in general; any thing eaten for nourishment.
The restriction of meat to the flesh of animals is a later and narrower use.
Greek sterea trophē, solid or firm nourishment, Hebrews 5:12.
Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, Hebrews 5:14.
Opposed to milk, the food of babes, Hebrews 5:13 and 1 Corinthians 3:2.
scriptures: Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Heb 5:13
For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
corruption_summary: Permanent milk is now the settled diet of much preaching, and the arrested appetite Hebrews rebukes as a fault is defended as accessibility.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern practice inverts the passage. Churches organise their teaching around the assumption that the congregation cannot bear doctrine, and so the first principles are repeated indefinitely under new packaging, with difficulty treated as a pastoral failure and depth as the preserve of specialists. Hebrews calls this condition a rebuke-worthy state, not a demographic fact. The readers ought by that time to have been teachers; the milk diet was the symptom of a stall. A ministry that has decided in advance that its people cannot digest the doctrine of justification, or the covenants, or the attributes of God, has made the babe-state permanent and called the arrangement kindness.

The error has a mirror image which is just as damaging. Some treat strong meat as a badge, so that doctrinal vocabulary becomes a mark of rank and the Christian who is still on milk is despised rather than fed. Hebrews gives no warrant for that either: the author's complaint is pastoral grief, and he goes on in the next chapter to urge his readers on to perfection rather than abandoning them. The text's own definition of maturity is also a rebuke to mere accumulation of information — those of full age are “those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.” Maturity is trained discernment, worked up by use, and a man who can define the terms but cannot tell good from evil in a live case has not yet eaten the meat. The principle to recover is that ordinary believers are meant for the deep things and must be fed accordingly.

pos: n. phr. (the lawlessness already at work in the world, awaiting its revealing)
etymology: Greek mystērion tēs anomias — mystērion, a secret disclosed by revelation, and anomia, lawlessness, from a, without, and nomos, law. The Authorized Version renders anomia as iniquity.
biblical_def: Writing to the Thessalonians about the day of the Lord, Paul says, “For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.” Each term carries weight. A mystery in the New Testament is not a puzzle but a thing hidden which God discloses; iniquity here translates anomia, lawlessness, the principle of being without law. The mystery of iniquity is therefore lawlessness working in concealment, present and operative but not yet unveiled. The tense is the arresting part: it doth already work, in Paul's own lifetime, long before the figure of verse three is revealed. Something restrains it — “he who now letteth will let”, where let is the old English for hinder, the opposite of its modern sense — and when that restraint is removed, “then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming.” Paul has already named the sequence: the day shall not come “except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition.” The passage therefore teaches a hidden continuity. Lawlessness is not an event scheduled for the end; it is a working principle in every age, held in check, moving toward an unveiling, and destined to be consumed by nothing more than the breath of Christ's mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Mystery, a profound secret; something hidden, and only to be known by revelation. Iniquity, injustice, unrighteousness, a deviation from rectitude. The mystery of iniquity, 2 Thessalonians 2:7, lawlessness at work in concealment.
webster_full: Mystery, a profound secret; something wholly unknown till revealed.
In Scripture, a truth hidden in God and made known by revelation.
Iniquity, want of equity; injustice, unrighteousness, wickedness.
Greek anomia, lawlessness, from a, without, and nomos, law.
The mystery of iniquity doth already work, 2 Thessalonians 2:7.
scriptures: For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.
Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;
And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming:
And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
corruption_summary: Lawlessness is reassigned to a future villain, so the present and hidden working Paul actually describes goes unexamined, while the word mystery is read as puzzle rather than as disclosure.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual handling pushes the whole passage into a future programme. In the dispensational scheme the restrainer is identified with the Holy Spirit withdrawn at a pre-tribulational rapture, the man of sin with a coming world ruler, and the mystery of iniquity with a season yet to begin. Whatever one concludes about the restrainer — and the Reformed tradition has read it variously as the Roman magistrate, ordered civil authority as such, or the preaching of the gospel — the scheme loses the verb Paul chose. The mystery already works. A reader who files lawlessness under the future has been excused from recognising it in his own institutions, his own church, and his own heart, which is precisely the vigilance the chapter was written to produce.

The second corruption is semantic and runs deep in modern usage. Mystery has come to mean an unsolved puzzle, and so the phrase is heard as an invitation to speculate; and iniquity has been softened into dysfunction, brokenness, or harm. Both shifts drain the phrase. A New Testament mystery is a secret God discloses, not a riddle men crack, so the right posture is attention to what has been revealed rather than conjecture about what has not. And anomia is a legal word: lawlessness is defiance of a real law given by a real Lawgiver, which is why Christ says of the last days that “because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.” The principle to recover is that the antidote to a hidden lawlessness is not prediction but obedience, and that its end is certain — consumed with the spirit of His mouth.

pos: n. phr. (the agent of Paul's thorn in the flesh, sent to buffet him)
etymology: Greek angelos Satana — angelos, a messenger or angel, and Satanas, from Hebrew satan, an adversary. The Authorized Version renders angelos here as messenger rather than angel.
biblical_def: Paul describes the affliction given him after his vision of paradise: “And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.” The Greek angelos is the ordinary word for angel, and the Authorized Version translates it messenger here because the sender is Satan. The verse holds together two things that are difficult to hold together, and the whole doctrine of the passage lies in their combination. The agent is satanic — this is an adversary's work, intended as a buffeting, which is the word for being struck with the fist. And yet the thing was given, a passive that names no human giver and points above Satan to God, and the purpose stated twice over is Paul's preservation from pride. The adversary strikes; the Father aims the blow. Paul besought the Lord thrice that it might depart, and the answer was not removal but sufficiency: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” What the messenger of Satan intended as destruction God employed as the very means of keeping an apostle humble and of displaying Christ's power. This is the book of Job's doctrine in a single verse: the adversary has real agency and no independence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Messenger, one who bears a message, an errand, or a dispatch. Satan, the grand adversary of man; the devil or prince of darkness. The messenger of Satan, 2 Corinthians 12:7, the agent of Paul's thorn in the flesh.
webster_full: Messenger, one who bears a message or an errand; a forerunner.
Greek angelos, a messenger, the same word elsewhere rendered angel.
Satan, from Hebrew satan, an adversary, an accuser, one who opposes.
The messenger of Satan to buffet me, 2 Corinthians 12:7.
Greek kolaphizō, to buffet, to strike with the fist.
scriptures: And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.
For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Job 2:6
And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life.
corruption_summary: The verse is pulled toward two opposite errors — a Christianity in which Satan acts outside God's government, and a therapeutic reading in which affliction has no purpose but to be removed.
corruption_paragraphs: The first distortion belongs to the health-and-prosperity teaching that treats every affliction as satanic in origin and therefore as something the believer must rebuke until it leaves. On that reading Paul simply lacked faith, and his thorn is an embarrassment to be explained away. The text forecloses it. Paul besought the Lord three times — the praying was right — and the Lord answered by refusing and by giving something better. A doctrine that cannot accommodate an unanswered apostolic prayer has set itself against the New Testament, and it leaves suffering Christians to conclude that their continuing affliction is their own fault.

The opposite distortion is quieter. In the therapeutic register, affliction is reduced to an experience to be processed and recovered from, with meaning supplied by the sufferer rather than by God; the question becomes how one copes, never what God intends. Paul's account is governed by purpose from first to last, and the purpose is stated twice in a single verse: lest I should be exalted above measure. The thorn is anti-pride medicine, prescribed by God and administered by an adversary who does not know he is being used. That is exactly the arrangement of Job 2:6, where Satan is given leave and given a limit in the same breath. The principle to recover is that the Christian under affliction may say both things at once without contradiction — the adversary struck me, and my Father sent it, and His grace is sufficient.

pos: n. phr. (the place to which Paul was caught up, identified with paradise)
etymology: Greek tritos ouranos — tritos, third, and ouranos, heaven or sky. Hebrew usage speaks of the heavens in the plural, whence the ascending senses of sky, starry expanse, and the dwelling-place of God.
biblical_def: Paul writes with deliberate indirection: “I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.” Two verses later he names the place again — “he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” — so that the third heaven and paradise are the same place under two names. The ordinal reflects the Hebrew way of speaking of the heavens in ascending senses: the air where the birds fly and the clouds gather, the expanse where the sun and stars are set, and above these the dwelling-place of God. To be caught up to the third is to be brought past both the others into the immediate presence of God. Three features of Paul's account govern its use. He speaks of himself in the third person, declining to make the experience a credential. He twice confesses ignorance of the mode — in the body or out of it, he cannot tell. And he reports that what he heard he is not permitted to repeat. The most extraordinary revelation in the apostolic record is thus deliberately withheld from the churches, and the chapter moves instead to a thorn, to weakness, and to sufficient grace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Heaven, the region of the air; the starry expanse; the dwelling-place of God and of the blessed. The third heaven, 2 Corinthians 12:2, the highest of these, identified in verse 4 with paradise.
webster_full: Heaven, the region of the air, where the clouds and birds are.
The expanse in which the sun, moon, and stars are set.
The dwelling-place of God, of angels, and of the blessed spirits.
The third heaven, 2 Corinthians 12:2, the highest of the three senses.
Identified with paradise in 2 Corinthians 12:4.
scriptures: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.
And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;)
How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities.
corruption_summary: A passage constructed to refuse spiritual celebrity is used to manufacture it, as heavenly-visit narratives are published for profit in defiance of Paul's express restraint.
corruption_paragraphs: The commercial heaven-visitation genre is the clearest modern contradiction of this text. Books reporting tours of the afterlife, with architecture, conversations, and messages brought back for publication, have sold in enormous numbers in evangelical markets, and each one does precisely what Paul declined to do. He spoke of himself in the third person; they trade on the first. He could not tell whether he was in the body; they supply confident detail. He was told the words were not lawful for a man to utter; they are printed and promoted. The contrast is not a matter of taste. Paul's restraint is argued, not accidental — he refuses to glory in the vision and glories instead in his infirmities, because the Corinthian church was being drawn after apostles who boasted of experiences.

A second and more academic error treats the three heavens as a cosmological claim to be measured against modern astronomy and then dismissed, as if Scripture were teaching a layered physical universe. The language is phenomenological and theological, naming the sky, the starry expanse, and the presence of God in ascending order, as Hebrew usage naturally does. Nothing in Paul depends upon a particular model of the cosmos. The principle to recover is the one the chapter itself enforces: genuine encounters with God produce reticence and humility, not platform; and the mark of a true messenger is that he directs attention away from his experiences to the sufficiency of grace.

pos: n. phr. (the appetite for teaching that gratifies rather than corrects)
etymology: Greek knēthomenoi tēn akoēn, literally being tickled as to the hearing, from knēthō, to scratch or tickle. The Authorized Version renders the sense as having itching ears.
biblical_def: Paul's charge to Timothy is given in view of a coming condition: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears.” The Greek figure is of an ear that itches and seeks scratching, and the mechanism Paul describes is worth tracing exactly, because the agency runs the wrong way from what is usually assumed. The hearers are not passive victims of bad teachers. They will not endure sound doctrine; they heap to themselves teachers; the teachers are gathered to meet a demand the hearers already have. The phrase after their own lusts names the engine: desire selects the teaching, and the teaching is then produced to satisfy the desire. Paul says the verb heap — they pile up teachers, accumulating as many as are needed until someone says the wanted thing. The outcome is stated in the next verse: “And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.” The remedy stands immediately before the diagnosis and is addressed to the preacher rather than the audience: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.” The man in the pulpit is to go on doing the unwanted thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Itching, a sensation in the skin causing a desire to scratch; figuratively, a teasing desire or longing. Itching ears, 2 Timothy 4:3, ears that crave gratifying rather than sound teaching.
webster_full: Itching, a peculiar sensation in the skin which inclines one to scratch.
Figuratively, a constant teasing desire or uneasy longing.
Greek knēthō, to scratch, to tickle; in the passive, to be tickled.
Having itching ears, 2 Timothy 4:3, of hearers who select their teachers.
The result is a turning from truth unto fables, 2 Timothy 4:4.
scriptures: For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
corruption_summary: The market has been given the pulpit, as preaching is shaped by what audiences will reward, and the verse's own assignment of blame to the hearers is quietly reversed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern form of the fault is structural rather than merely personal. Where a ministry's survival depends on attendance, subscription, or engagement, the hearers' preferences acquire real authority over the content preached, and the sorting Paul describes happens automatically and without anyone intending it. Teaching that reproves and rebukes performs poorly by every metric a platform reports; teaching that gratifies performs well; and the mechanism heaps up teachers after the hearers' own lusts just as the verse says. The analytics do what the itching ear used to have to do by hand.

It should be said plainly that this is not an argument for harshness, nor a licence for the preacher who has mistaken his own abrasiveness for faithfulness. Paul's instruction in the previous verse pairs reproof and rebuke with all longsuffering and doctrine, and a man who enjoys wounding his people is not obeying it. Nor does the passage condemn a hearer for wanting to be fed; it condemns an appetite that has made itself the judge of the menu. The principle to recover is the order of authority. The word is preached in season and out of season, which means that its seasonableness is not determined by the audience; and the hearer's part, according to the Bereans whom Scripture commends, is to search the Scriptures to see whether the things preached are so — not to search the teachers until one is found who is pleasing.

pos: n. phr. (the governing principle of sin in the flesh, from which Christ frees)
etymology: Greek ho nomos tēs hamartias kai tou thanatou — nomos, law, used here of a governing principle or operative rule rather than of the Mosaic code.
biblical_def: Paul writes, “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.” The word law carries a particular sense in this stretch of Romans. It is not primarily the Mosaic code but a governing principle, a rule that operates with the regularity of a law, as when a man says that a body falls by a law. Paul has already described the thing from the inside: “But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.” That is the law of sin — an operative principle resident in the flesh, which does not merely tempt but brings into captivity. It is joined to death because death is what it pays, as Paul says elsewhere that the wages of sin is death. The verse is a liberation formula, and the structure matters: one law is overcome by another law, not by effort. Freedom does not come from the captive's resolve but from a superior operative principle, “the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus”, which is the indwelling Spirit working with the same regularity on the other side. The preceding verse supplies the ground on which the whole stands: “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” Deliverance is announced as accomplished — hath made me free, a past act with a standing result.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Law, a rule of action; also, in a more general sense, the established order or operation of any thing. The law of sin and death, Romans 8:2, the governing principle of sin in the flesh, whose wages is death.
webster_full: Law, a rule of action prescribed by a superior authority.
In a larger sense, the settled and regular order of operation of any thing.
Greek nomos, used by Paul of an operative principle, Romans 7:23.
The law of sin which is in my members, Romans 7:23.
Overcome by the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:2.

For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.
Rom 7:23

Rom 8:1

Rom 6:23

corruption_summary: Sin is redescribed as a wound rather than a reigning principle, so that the deliverance Paul announces as accomplished by a superior law is replaced with self-management.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic anthropology has largely replaced the Pauline one in popular teaching. Sin becomes brokenness, dysfunction, or unmet need; the sinner becomes principally a sufferer; and the remedy becomes insight, self-acceptance, and better habits. The pastoral motive is often genuine, and Scripture does speak tenderly of the bruised reed, so this is not an argument for harshness toward the afflicted. But the substitution removes the category Paul is actually working with. The law of sin is not a wound; it is a rule in the members that brings a man into captivity, and captives are not healed by insight. They are freed, by someone else, from outside.

The mirror error is moralism, which keeps the language of sin and loses the language of law. Here sin is treated as a series of bad choices to be corrected by resolve, accountability, and effort, so that the Christian life becomes a programme of self-improvement under grace-flavoured vocabulary. Romans 8:2 forecloses both by its grammar. One law is displaced by another law; freedom comes from the law of the Spirit of life, not from the believer's struggle; and the verb is past — hath made me free. The principle to recover is that deliverance from indwelling sin is a work of the indwelling Spirit grounded in a verdict already passed, that there is therefore now no condemnation. Mortification follows that verdict and never produces it.

pos: n. phr. (the mutual belonging of believers as limbs of one body)
etymology: Greek melēethe allēlōn — melos, a limb or member of the body, and allēlōn, of one another. The English member here keeps its older anatomical sense of a bodily limb.
biblical_def: Paul uses the phrase twice. In Romans: “So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another.” In Ephesians it grounds a command about speech: “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.” The English word member has weakened into a term for someone enrolled on a list, but the Greek melos means a limb, and the whole argument depends on the stronger sense. Believers are not members of a church the way men are members of a club, by subscription and at will; they are limbs of a body, joined by life and not by decision, and a limb has no existence apart from the body it belongs to. Paul develops the figure at length in the first Corinthian letter: “For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.” Two consequences follow in the apostle's own reasoning. Difference is necessary rather than regrettable, since a body made of one kind of limb is not a body. And injury is shared, so that lying is forbidden on the ground stated — a man who deceives his brother is a hand deceiving its own body. The phrase is therefore not a sentiment about warm fellowship but a statement about what the church is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Member, a limb of an animal body; a part of a whole. Members one of another, Romans 12:5, the mutual belonging of believers as limbs of one body in Christ.
webster_full: Member, a limb of an animal body; a part of a discourse or a whole.
Greek melos, a limb or member of the body.
We, being many, are one body in Christ, Romans 12:5.
Every one members one of another, the ground of truthful speech, Ephesians 4:25.

corruption_summary: Church membership has been reduced to a voluntary affiliation held at will, so a phrase describing limbs of one body is read as a description of a club's roster.
corruption_paragraphs: The consumer model of church life is the direct contradiction of this phrase. A congregation is approached as a provider of services to be evaluated and exchanged, attendance is kept provisional, and formal membership is declined as unnecessary or treated as a mere formality. The arrangement is defended on the ground that the church is people rather than an institution, which is true and beside the point, since Paul's figure is not institutional but organic and binds more tightly rather than less. A limb does not evaluate its body. The same instinct produces the unattached Christian who follows teaching online and belongs nowhere in particular, which on this figure is not a reduced form of church life but a severed limb.

The error has a counterpart that must be named as well, because the figure cuts both ways. Leaders who use body language to demand compliance, to suppress legitimate dissent, or to make departure from a congregation feel like apostasy have taken Paul's organic image and used it as a chain. Nothing in the passage supports that. The apostle's own applications are protective of the weaker member and insistent that the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee. The principle to recover is mutual belonging with teeth: that truth-telling is owed because we are limbs of one body, that the suffering of one member is the suffering of all, and that this belonging is created by union with Christ rather than by joining.

pos: n. phr. (the gesture by which the Jerusalem apostles recognised Paul's commission)
etymology: Greek dexias koinōnias — dexia, the right hand, and koinōnia, fellowship or partnership. The right hand was the ancient pledge of covenant and good faith.
biblical_def: The phrase belongs to Paul's account of his dealings with the Jerusalem leadership: “And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.” The Authorized Version has the plural hands, which the modern idiom usually drops. The gesture is a covenantal one: in the ancient world the right hand given was the pledge of good faith, and here it functions as a formal public recognition. What is recognised is carefully specified. They perceived the grace that was given unto Paul — the acknowledgment is of God's work, not of Paul's qualifications, and the preceding verse says the ground was that they saw the gospel of the uncircumcision had been committed to him. The outcome is a division of field rather than of message: Paul and Barnabas to the heathen, the Jerusalem apostles to the circumcision, with one gospel between them. The setting gives the gesture its weight, since this is the same chapter in which Paul withstands Peter to the face at Antioch. The right hands of fellowship are therefore not a token of sentimental agreement among men who never differ. They are a recognition, between men who did sharply differ, of a common gospel and a shared work.

corruption_summary: Fellowship has been reduced to friendliness and refreshments, so a covenantal pledge recognising a divine commission is heard as a handshake of general goodwill.
corruption_paragraphs: In common church usage fellowship now names the hour after the service and the food served at it. The New Testament word is koinōnia, a sharing in something held in common, and in Galatians 2 the thing held in common is the gospel itself. When the word is emptied of content, the gesture it describes is emptied too, and the right hand of fellowship becomes a welcome extended on the basis of pleasantness rather than of truth. The Jerusalem apostles did not give Paul their hands because he was agreeable; they gave them because they perceived the grace of God in his commission and saw that the same gospel had been committed to him.

A second corruption runs the other way, and the same chapter rebukes it. Because Paul withstood Peter to the face at Antioch, some have taken the passage as a warrant for a separatism that withholds recognition from every brother who differs in anything. But both events are in Galatians 2, and they are not in tension: the same apostle who gave and received the right hands of fellowship over a shared gospel rebuked an apostle publicly when conduct contradicted that gospel. Recognition rests on the gospel; rebuke is owed when the gospel is compromised; and neither is a matter of temperament. The principle to recover is that fellowship is a covenantal word with a doctrinal floor, extended on the ground of grace perceived, and that recognising a man's commission and correcting his conduct are both acts of the same fidelity.

pos: n. phr. (the third of the three worldly appetites named in 1 John 2:16)
etymology: Greek hē alazoneia tou biou — alazoneia, vainglory or boastful pretension, from alazōn, a braggart; and bios, life in the sense of livelihood, means, and manner of living, as distinct from zōē, life itself.
biblical_def: John names three things and says of all of them that they are not of the Father: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.” The third is the subtlest, and the Greek is precise. Alazoneia is the pretension of a braggart, the posture of a man displaying what he has or claims to have; and bios is not life in itself but life as a mode of living — one's means, standing, and circumstances. The pride of life is therefore vainglory about one's manner of life: position, security, possessions, and the appearance of being well established. It differs from the first two in its object. The lust of the flesh wants to consume, and the lust of the eyes wants to acquire; the pride of life wants to be seen to have, which is why it can flourish in a man who has disciplined the other two. The command governing all three stands just before: “Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” John then supplies the argument from durability: “And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.” The case against the pride of life is finally not that display is distasteful but that the thing displayed is passing away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Pride, inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority. The pride of life, 1 John 2:16, vain-glory in one's condition, means, and manner of living.
webster_full: Pride, inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's superiority.

corruption_summary: Display of one's manner of life has been industrialised and renamed as personal brand, so that the exact disposition John forbids is now an ordinary professional requirement.
corruption_paragraphs: The curated public life is the pride of life at scale. Platforms are built to reward the display of one's circumstances — the house, the holiday, the position, the family arranged for the photograph — and the display is measured and paid in attention. Everything in the apparatus is tuned to alazoneia, vainglory about one's bios. What is new is not the sin, which is as old as the braggart John had in view, but its normalisation: a man is now expected to maintain a presentation of his life as a condition of ordinary employment, and to decline is treated as a professional failure rather than as restraint. That pressure is real and a Christian may have to live under it, but he should not be deceived about what it is pulling at.

The error is doubled when the same instinct is sanctified. Ministry success, family photographs, conference platforms, and the public performance of piety are all available to be displayed, and Scripture reserves its sharpest words for exactly this version — the trumpet sounded before the alms, the prayer made to be seen. Nor is the remedy a staged modesty, which is simply vainglory in a plainer coat. John's remedy is comparative and it is about duration: the world passeth away, and the lust thereof, but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever. The principle to recover is that display is vain because its object is perishing, and the cure is not contempt for good things but an affection fixed on what remains.

pos: n. phr. (the appetite of fallen nature, set against the Spirit)
etymology: Greek hē epithymia tēs sarkos — epithymia, strong desire or craving, from epi, upon, and thymos, passion; and sarx, flesh, used by Paul of fallen human nature rather than of the body as such.
biblical_def: The phrase stands in two apostles. John lists it first of the three things that are in the world: “the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.” Paul sets it against the Spirit as the alternative to a walk: “This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.” Two matters of definition govern the phrase. Lust in the Authorized Version is not confined to sexual desire; epithymia is strong craving of any kind, and the same word is used of a good longing in Luke 22:15. And flesh in Paul is not the body. The body is God's workmanship and is to be presented as a living sacrifice; sarx names human nature as fallen, the self in its independence from God, which is why the works of the flesh listed in the same chapter include hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, and heresies alongside the sins of appetite. Paul then describes a real and unresolved conflict in the believer: “For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.” The remedy given is not suppression but direction — walk in the Spirit, a positive occupation — grounded in an accomplished fact: “they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”

corruption_summary: Desire is now treated as self-authenticating, so that to question an appetite is heard as an attack on identity; while an older error reads flesh as the body and slanders what God made.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning assumption of the age is that a desire, by being deeply felt, is thereby justified and constitutes the self. On that premise the language of lust is unintelligible except as cruelty, since to call a craving disordered is to call the person disordered. Scripture holds the opposite: desires are to be judged by a standard outside themselves, the heart is deceitful above all things, and a man's strongest wants are precisely what most need examining. This does not make desire evil as such — the same Greek word describes Christ's own longing to eat the passover with His disciples — and Christian teaching here must be honest that the issue is the object and the authority of desire, not the fact of wanting. But a gospel that cannot say any appetite is wrong has nothing to say to a man enslaved by one.

The ancient error ran the other way, and it has never fully died. Reading flesh as the body, Christians have abused the body as the seat of sin, which produced monastic self-mutilation, a suspicion of marriage and food and beauty, and a piety measured by deprivation. Paul's own list refutes it, since the works of the flesh include hatred, variance, emulations, strife, and heresies — sins of the mind and the temper that no fasting touches. A cold, censorious, doctrinally precise man may be walking wholly in the flesh. The principle to recover is Paul's positive remedy: the answer to the lust of the flesh is not hatred of the body but occupation of the whole man in the Spirit, resting on the fact that those who are Christ's have already crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts.
